To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

spoken-only presentations are inferior to spoken–written presentations and that spoken–written presentations are superior to written-only presentations, but only when learning is system-paced, when learners have low prior knowledge, or when animations or diagrams are not present.

the concurrent presentation of verbatim spoken narration and onscreen text does not improve learning outcomes compared with the concurrent presentation of onscreen text only, and that the concurrent presentation is superior to the presentation of verbatim narration alone, especially for low prior knowledge students, when learning is paced by the computer and there are no accompanying animations or diagrams.
spoken–written presentations are superior to spoken-only presentations, and that spoken–written and spoken-only presentations are equally effective as written-only presentations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the use of speech, written text and animation can be optimally combined to support learning from multimedia presentations.
the effects of verbal redundancy in the context of multimedia learning.
the effects of verbal redundancy in multimedia learning environments, that is, the concurrent presentation of speech and text.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
spoken–written presentations are better than spoken-only presentations, and that key term displays are better than verbatim displays.

spoken-only, written–only, and spoken– written presentations do not differ in terms of learning retention, and that spoken–written presentations are superior to spoken-only presentations in terms of learning transfer, particularly for low prior knowledge, system-paced, and picture-free learning materials.
spoken–written presentations are better than spoken-only and written-only presentations for most learners in most situations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
spoken narration should not be used in conjunction with verbatim text.
the inclusion of text with narration is beneficial to learning, but only when text is not verbatim.
spoken-only presentations are less effective than written-only and spoken–written ones, and that spoken–written ones are less effective than those with key terms.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, for learning from multimedia materials, spoken-only is not better than written-only, and the combination of spoken and written information is not necessarily superior to either presentation alone.

spoken–written presentations are not always more effective than spoken-only presentations, and that the use of key words is a better strategy than verbatim narration for enhancing learning from multimedia materials.
, when designing multimedia learning materials, it is better to use spoken–written presentation rather than spoken-only or written-only presentation.
